title: Securing zero-copy distribution patterns with OneLake security and shortcuts
summary: Fabric Updates Blog post giving architectural design guidance for choosing between pass-through and delegated OneLake shortcuts when distributing data at scale. Overlaps heavily with the shortcuts and security sources already in this KB; the material captured here is limited to the intersection security rule for delegated shortcuts, the design-choice framing, and the external-shortcut identity clarification not already recorded.
audience: Data platform architects designing governed, multi-team or multi-tenant data distribution on OneLake who must choose between pass-through and delegated shortcut security models.
why_it_matters: Gives explicit architectural decision criteria (not just mechanics) for when to use pass-through versus delegated shortcuts, and clarifies the precise security composition rule (intersection, most-restrictive-wins) that governs delegated shortcut access - detail useful for security review sign-off.
takeaways: Delegated shortcut access is the intersection of permissions granted to the delegated identity and permissions granted to the end user - the end user can never exceed what the delegated identity itself was granted.
Pass-through shortcuts remain the recommended default for collaborative engineering scenarios where per-person, source-managed authorization must stay consistent regardless of access path.
Delegated shortcuts are recommended specifically when managing individual end-user access on the source becomes an operational bottleneck at scale, or when sharing across a Fabric tenant boundary.

External shortcuts to non-Fabric stores (S3, Google Cloud Storage) are themselves a form of delegated shortcut, where the delegated identity is typically an account key or system identity in the external system.

claims.text: For delegated OneLake shortcuts, access is computed as the intersection of what the delegated identity is permitted to see and what OneLake security grants the end user, so an end user can never be given more access than the delegated identity itself was authorized for.

The recommended design pattern for delegating access to thousands of downstream users is to represent each consuming team or region with its own service principal, scope that service principal to only its slice of the data, and let the team's own owners manage individual end-user permissions behind that service principal.

Design guidance from the post: choose pass-through shortcuts when the goal is letting multiple teams reuse a shared dataset while preserving strict source-managed, per-person authorization; choose delegated shortcuts when the goal is broader curated distribution where centralizing per-user provisioning on the source does not scale.

External shortcuts to non-Fabric stores such as AWS S3 and Google Cloud Storage are themselves categorized as a form of delegated shortcut, where the delegated identity is typically an account key or system identity native to the external system rather than a Fabric organizational account or service principal.

For pass-through shortcuts, OneLake security cannot be additionally configured on the shortcut path itself; access is evaluated only at the target so the data owner retains full, exclusive control over who can read the data regardless of which shortcut path is used to reach it.

The post frames a shortcut used in delegated mode as becoming part of a governed publishing architecture: the central team keeps ownership of the source, consuming teams avoid copying data, and downstream users get a managed access experience rather than direct raw-path access to the source item.
